stem: Veena always consumes y=3x and pₓ=3pᵧ. She owns18 units x and78 units y, tradable at market prices, with no other income. How much x does she buy from the market?
answer: C:4 units of net x purchases.
solution: Value the endowment in units of the y price: income is3·18+78=132. Her fixed ratio costs3x+3x=6x, so final x=22,y66. She buys22−18=4 units x and finances it by selling12 units y. Final consumption22 is not the requested net purchase.
hint: Value the endowment and distinguish final demand from net trade.
options: Cannot determine without the absolute price of x

stem: Utility is U(C,M/P), depending on consumption C and real balances M/P. Budget is PC+M=M̄, where M̄ is initial nominal wealth. What is the substitution effect of higher P on C?
solution: In real units the budget is C+M/P=M̄/P. Consumption and real balances always have the same relative price1, so higher P changes real wealth but not the relative price between utility arguments. Pure substitution effect is zero; any consumption change is a real-income effect.
hint: Divide the nominal budget by P.

stem: A monopolist has no fixed cost, MC5 and demand D(p)=10/p if0<p≤10, zero ifp>10. Only integer outputs are possible. Find optimal output.
solution: Positive output q≥1 can sell at p=10/q, generating revenue10. Profit is10−5q, largest at the smallest positive integerq1, where profit5 exceeds shutdown profit0.
hint: Revenue is constant across positive feasible integer outputs.

stem: Domestic production of capital goods rises by100, of which80 are sold and20 unsold. Imports of capital goods simultaneously decline by30. Everything else is unchanged. By how much does GDP rise?
solution: Domestic current production adds100 to GDP, including unsold inventory20. For expenditure accounting, domestic capital-goods purchases rise80, inventory investment rises20 and imported capital-goods purchases fall30, so total investment changes by70. Subtracting imports, whose change is−30, gives ΔGDP=70−(−30)=100. Adding the import decline to domestic production without adjusting investment would double count.
hint: Include inventories and remove imported investment consistently.
notes: Handwritten ticks in the scan are not an official answer key and are not used.

stem: A consumer buys X,Y. Y costs pᵧ; X can be bought at a high price p_H or a lower price p_L available only after t hours of search. He normally works8 hours daily at wage w. (i) Describe the budget set and an equilibrium choosing the lower price. (ii) Can higher w make him choose the higher price?
answer: Budget is the union of p_Hx+pᵧy≤8w and p_Lx+pᵧy≤(8−t)w, if search displaces work. Yes, higher wages can make shopping time too costly.
solution: Assuming0<t<8 and search replaces paid work, high-price purchase preserves income8w, whereas searching costswt in foregone earnings. The two lines cross at x*=wt/(p_H−p_L); their upper envelope uses the high-price line below the crossing and the low-price line above it. Draw a highest indifference curve tangent to the exposed low-price branch to depict that choice. A wage rise increases the opportunity costwt. For a concrete switch, take pᵧ1,p_H2,p_L1,t1 and U=log x+y. When affordable, high-price optimum x=.5 gives indirect utility8w−1−log2; low-price optimum x1 gives7w−1. Searching is preferred iffw<log2. Thusw=.5 leads to searching, butw1 leads to high-price purchase. Homothetic preferences need not generate this switch because both budget sets scale together with w; possibility, not necessity, is the claim.
hint: Price savings must compensate for foregone wages while searching.
notes: The source does not explicitly say search reduces paid work; this opportunity-cost interpretation is stated.

stem: Telephone planA costs fixed500 plus2 per call; planB costs fixed1000 plus1 per call. Three consumers have identical incomes: one choosesA, oneB, one neither. (i) Describe budget contours and indifference curves for these choices. (ii) Could the non-subscriber have an ordinary Cobb–Douglas utility over calls and other consumption?
answer: With other consumption as numeraire: A gives o=M−500−2q, B gives o=M−1000−q; no subscription gives(q,o)=(0,M). The third cannot have Cobb–Douglas utility with strictly positive exponents when a positive-call plan is affordable.
solution: The two plan lines intersect atq500,o=M−1500. A is cheaper below500 calls; B is cheaper above500. Draw the upper feasible envelope together with the separate no-subscription point(0,M). A highest attainable indifference curve can touchA for the first person, B for the second, or the no-subscription point for someone valuing calls little. For U=q^αo^β withα,β>0, no subscription gives utility0. A feasible positive-call, positive-other-consumption bundle gives positive utility, so it dominates. The shared income permits planB for another consumer and therefore makes such a positive bundle underA affordable. Hence an ordinary two-good Cobb–Douglas function cannot represent the third consumer’s stated choice; a shifted or satiation-based utility might.
hint: Include the discrete no-subscription option outside the two subscription lines.

stem: A buyer has one50-rupee note. Rice and pulses are sold at prices p_r,p_p. The rice seller gives change only if at least3kg rice is bought; the pulses seller never gives change. (i) Describe the budget. (ii) Find the optimum for fixed-proportion consumption. (iii) Find the maximum fee an outside money changer could charge. (iv) How does a pulses-price rise affect purchases and the fee?
answer: Under the standard rice-first/change interpretation, ordinary trade with both goods requires rice≥3. Let desired ratio be(r,p)=(az,bz). If the unconstrained rice demand is below3, z₀=(50−3p_r)/(bp_p), and maximal change fee is F_max=50−(ap_r+bp_p)z₀. In that binding region higher p_p reduces z₀ and raises F_max.
solution: Assume3p_r≤50 and that rice purchase≥3 provides usable change for a subsequent pulse purchase. The attainable frontier for both goods is the ordinary line p_rr+p_pp=50 truncated tor≥3, plus one-good spending possibilities. Without the restriction, fixed-proportion demand would bez*=50/(ap_r+bp_p). Ifaz*≥3 this is attainable and the change service has no value. Ifaz*<3, buying minimum rice3 leaves pulses(50−3p_r)/p_p, so Leontief utility in bundle units isz₀=(50−3p_r)/(bp_p), with some rice wasted relative to the preferred ratio. Paying feeF restores a standard budget50−F and balanced consumptionz_F=(50−F)/(ap_r+bp_p). The highest acceptable fee solvesz_F=z₀, giving F_max=50−(ap_r+bp_p)z₀≥0. At exactly that fee the buyer is indifferent; a slightly smaller fee induces strict use. In the binding region and3p_r<50, dz₀/dp_p<0 and dF_max/dp_p=ap_r(50−3p_r)/(bp_p²)>0. Without changing money rice stays3 and pulses fall; with a fully extracting changer both balanced quantitiesaz₀,bz₀ fall. Cash denominations, the possibility of exact payments and the ratio are not supplied, so the answer is explicitly conditional rather than a unique numerical purchase.
hint: Compare utility under the minimum-rice restriction with utility under an ordinary budget reduced by a fee.
notes: Cash/change mechanics are incomplete, and prices and desired ratio are unspecified. The standard continuous-goods, rice-first interpretation is explicit; source repeats subpart label(iii).

stem: Each other street-garbage dumper imposes costa, so the external harm to a person is an, where n is the number of other dumpers and a>0. Dumping oneself yields benefitG and private costC/n, C>0. (a) Explain no dumping ifn0. (b) Find the threshold number of other dumpers making dumping optimal.
answer: ForG>0, dump iff n≥C/G; the least positive integer threshold is ceiling(C/G). It depends onC andG, not a. At n0 the printed costC/n requires a limiting convention.
solution: Others’ harman is borne whether or not the person herself dumps, so it cancels from her comparison. The incremental payoff from dumping isG−C/n. Forn>0 this is nonnegative iff n≥C/G; equality gives indifference. Interpret the private cost as tending to infinity asn approaches0 from above, or define solitary dumping as prohibitively costly, to obtain the intended no-dumping result atn0. LiterallyC/0 is undefined, so the source needs that convention for part(a). A largerC raises the threshold, a largerG lowers it, and the external-damage coefficienta has no effect on this private threshold.
hint: Compare the incremental private payoffs; others’ pollution is common to both options.
notes: The printed costC/n is undefined atn0. Intended infinite-cost limiting interpretation is stated explicitly.

stem: Consumption depends only on income, investment only on interest, and G is exogenous. A unit rise in G shifts IS vertically upward by.5 at every income. Find dI/dr.
solution: IS isY=C(Y)+I(r)+G. HoldingY fixed while varyingG gives0=I′(r)dr+dG, so dr/dG=−1/I′. A unit increase shiftingr upward by.5 gives.5=−1/I′ and therefore I′=−2.
hint: Hold income fixed when interpreting the vertical shift.

stem: In a simple Keynesian economy without government, planned investment is7. AtY0, consumption is one-half of planned aggregate demand. AtY30, unplanned inventory accumulation is5. Find the autonomous-spending multiplier.
answer: Multiplier30/19, assuming an affine consumption schedule.
solution: LetC=a+bY andE=C+7. AtY0, a/(a+7)=1/2 givesa7 andE014. AtY30, output exceeds planned demand by5, soE(30)=25. Henceb=(25−14)/30=11/30. The autonomous-spending multiplier is1/(1−b)=30/19.
hint: Unplanned inventory accumulation meansY exceeds planned demand.
notes: Question starts on PDFpage6 and continues on PDFpage2 because of the booklet’s unusual scan order. Linear consumption is the usual simple-Keynesian interpretation.

stem: A project costs200 now and pays100 per year from next year onward. Each year, conditional on survival, abandonment permanently occurs with probability1/4. At a10% annual discount rate, is investment profitable?
answer: Yes. If abandonment occurs before each payment, PV=1500/7≈214.286 and NPV=100/7≈14.286.
solution: With survival probabilityq=.75 and discount factor1/1.1, expected year-t revenue is100qᵗ if the first payment also requires survival. PV=100Σ(t≥1)(q/1.1)ᵗ=100q/(1.1−q)=1500/7. Subtracting200 gives positive NPV100/7. If the first payment is guaranteed and abandonment is tested after payments, PV=100/(1.1−q)=2000/7 and NPV600/7, also positive. The investment recommendation is unchanged by this timing convention.
notes: Interprets abandonment probability as a constant conditional annual hazard; both common within-year payment timings give a positive NPV.

stem: A firm producesy=x₁x₂ with positive input pricesr₁,r₂. If minimized production cost is4, findy.
solution: For targety, minimum cost ismin(r₁x₁+r₂x₂) subject tox₁x₂≥y. AM–GM givescost≥2√(r₁r₂y), attained whenr₁x₁=r₂x₂. Equating minimized cost4 givesr₁r₂y4, so y=4/(r₁r₂). At the optimum each input’s expenditure is2.
hint: Use AM–GM or equalize the two input expenditures.
